summaryZh: 本文探讨了第一代农业田间机器人进入二手市场后引发的估值难题：机器人高度依赖软件、连接性和厂商支持，其残值评估远比传统农机复杂。文章分析了二手市场对小型农户降低自主农业门槛的潜在推动作用，同时指出软件许可转让、厂商存续风险和硬件技术过时等核心不确定性，并呼吁金融机构关注机器人残值评估问题。
featuredReason: 本文直面农业机器人商业化落地的关键瓶颈——二手残值与软件支持问题，对智慧畜牧行业评估机器人投资回报、制定设备更新策略及理解金融机构风控逻辑具有重要参考价值。
contentFull:
Can second-hand robots make autonomous farming affordable for smaller growers?

 05-10 | Field robots | Expert opinion

LinkedInFacebookXWhatsAppPrint

 

 Geert Hekkert Chief editor of Future Farming

Photo: Generated with AI

The first generation of agricultural field robots is slowly finding its way onto the second-hand market. This raises an interesting question: what will an agricultural robot actually be worth after 5 or 10 years, or even after 30 years?

With tractors, combines and other farm machinery, we have a fairly good idea. Age, operating hours, maintenance, brand and technical condition all provide a reasonable indication of residual value. With agricultural robots, we still have to discover how this will work. They are a new breed in the world of farm machinery, and one that has only just learned to stand on its own feet.

So when does a robot actually become old? A tractor can easily last 30 years or more, particularly older, analogue machines that are not dependent on software updates. With robots, things are fundamentally different. And that immediately creates one of the biggest uncertainties for anyone considering a used robot.

To address those concerns, robot manufacturers promise long-term software support and opportunities to upgrade their machines. Naïo, for example, can equip older Oz robots with new hardware, GPS and a modem. Other manufacturers also try to keep their robots up to date through software and hardware upgrades. In principle, a robot built in 2022 could therefore still offer almost the same functionality as a newer machine many years later.

But the opposite is also possible. Cameras, GPUs, LiDAR and AI are developing at tremendous speed. At some point, new software may no longer run on older hardware. A robot that is mechanically in excellent condition could then still become technologically obsolete. Much like a smartphone: it still works, but the latest software will no longer run on it.

Second-hand market could accelerate adoption

A healthy second-hand market could meanwhile give robot adoption a significant boost, particularly among smaller growers. Those unwilling or unable to immediately invest €100,000 or several hundred thousand euros could get started with autonomous farming much more cheaply through a used machine. Just as generations of farmers bought their first larger tractor, self-propelled sprayer or combine second-hand.

But what are you actually buying when you buy a used robot?

For me, that is still the big unknown. Robots depend much more heavily on software, connectivity, service contracts and subscriptions than traditional farm machinery. Will software licences and subscriptions transfer without restrictions to a second or third owner? And will manufacturers continue supporting older generations?

And what happens if the manufacturer no longer exists ten years from now? Many robot manufacturers are still relatively small and vulnerable companies. In recent years, the sector has already seen several manufacturers disappear or run into financial difficulties. A used tractor will usually keep running regardless. But what happens to a robot that depends on its manufacturer for updates, software or cloud connectivity?

Operating hours may also take on a different meaning. Burro reports robots clocking up 20,000 to 30,000 hours in just four years. After all, autonomy makes it possible to accumulate many more operating hours in a relatively short period. But electric motors and gearboxes still wear out. A robot could therefore use up its technical lifespan faster than a tractor.

Manufacturers that continue supporting older machines, make upgrades possible and allow software to be transferred to new owners could therefore gain an important advantage. Just as with cars and tractors, a strong reputation on the second-hand market can also help sell new robots.

But ultimately, someone has to put a value on that used machine. And that makes me particularly curious about a party we rarely hear from in discussions about agricultural robots: the financier. How will a bank determine the residual value of a €200,000 or €300,000 robot that may still be mechanically sound five years from now, but for which nobody knows whether its software will still be supported?

translationZh:
第一代农业田间机器人正慢慢进入二手市场。这引发了一个有趣的问题：一台农业机器人在5年、10年甚至30年后究竟还值多少钱？

对于拖拉机、联合收割机和其他农业机械，我们已经有相当清晰的认知。机龄、工作小时数、维护状况、品牌和技术状况都能为残值提供合理参考。而对于农业机器人，我们仍需探索其规律。它们是农机世界中的新物种，而且才刚刚学会独立行走。

那么，机器人什么时候才算“老”？一台拖拉机可以轻松使用30年甚至更久，尤其是不依赖软件更新的老式模拟机器。但机器人则完全不同。这立即为任何考虑购买二手机器人的人带来了最大的不确定性之一。

为了解决这些顾虑，机器人制造商承诺提供长期软件支持和对机器进行升级的机会。例如，Naïo可以为较老的Oz机器人配备新硬件、GPS和调制解调器。其他制造商也试图通过软件和硬件升级来保持其机器人的更新。原则上，一台2022年制造的机器人在多年后仍可能提供与更新机器几乎相同的功能。

但相反的情况也可能发生。摄像头、GPU、LiDAR和AI正在飞速发展。到了某个时候，新软件可能无法在旧硬件上运行。一台机械状况极佳的机器人届时仍可能在技术上过时。就像智能手机一样：它还能用，但最新软件已无法在其上运行。

**二手市场可能加速采用**

一个健康的二手市场 meanwhile 可能显著推动机器人的采用，尤其是在小型种植者中。那些不愿或无法立即投资10万欧元或数十万欧元的人，可以通过二手机器以低得多的成本开始自主农业。正如几代农民通过二手购买他们的第一台大型拖拉机、自走式喷雾机或联合收割机一样。

但当你购买一台二手机器人时，你实际买到的到底是什么？

对我来说，这仍然是最大的未知数。机器人比传统农业机械更严重地依赖软件、连接性、服务合同和订阅。软件许可证和订阅能否无限制地转让给第二或第三任所有者？制造商是否会继续支持老一代产品？

如果制造商十年后不复存在了怎么办？许多机器人制造商仍然是相对小型和脆弱的公司。近年来，该行业已经有多家制造商消失或陷入财务困境。一台二手拖拉机通常还能继续运行。但一台依赖制造商提供更新、软件或云连接的机器人会怎样？

工作小时数也可能具有不同的含义。Burro报告称，机器人在短短四年内就累计了2万到3万工作小时。毕竟，自主性使得在相对较短的时间内积累更多工作小时成为可能。但电动机和变速箱仍然会磨损。因此，一台机器人可能比拖拉机更快地耗尽技术寿命。

那些继续支持老机器、使升级成为可能并允许软件转让给新所有者的制造商，可能会获得重要优势。正如汽车和拖拉机一样，在二手市场上拥有良好声誉也有助于销售新机器人。

但最终，必须有人为那台二手机器定价。这让我特别好奇一个在农业机器人讨论中很少听到的参与方：融资方。银行将如何确定一台价值20万或30万欧元的机器人的残值——五年后它可能机械状况仍然良好，但没人知道其软件是否还会被支持？
